A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same FormalBench study. Their main text, equations, tables, figures and appendices are readable and support comparison, including matching relocated material from v1 Appendices A-I to v4 Appendices A-J.

before.justification: V1 reports original LLM benchmarking, prompting comparisons, robustness experiments, failure analysis and self-repair results in Section 4, Tables 1-2, Figures 3-4 and the appendices.

after.justification: V4 retains these original experiments and adds model evaluations, human validation of completeness scores, an equivalent-mutant audit, cost analysis and specification case studies.

M1.justification: The benchmark construction, 18 transformations, verification and mutation-analysis procedures, prompting methods and classifier-guided self-repair remain unchanged. V1's generation and repair prompts are retained in v4 Appendices I-J.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate Java/JML specification inference using the same 700-program FormalBench-Base, 6,219-program augmented collection and 1,794-transformation robustness subset. The added validation samples and case studies remain within this coverage.

E2.justification: Table 1 adds Qwen2.5-32B, Qwen2.5-72B, Llama3-70B and two distilled DeepSeek-R1 models. It also reidentifies the DeepSeek-V2-236B block as DeepSeekCoder-33B-Instruct, consistent with the revised Appendix C. O3-mini and SpecGen mutation-based repair already appeared in v1.

E3.justification: V4 adds low/high o3-mini reasoning settings, human assessment of 20 specifications with 66 pairwise comparisons, a 20-program mutant audit and cost-per-task evaluation. Table 1 also revises the declared DeepSeek configuration from 236B V2 to 33B Coder; identical scores and retained V2 wording in Section 4.2 prevent inferring a rerun. The stated temperature and token limit remain 0.7 and 2048.

E4.justification: New analyses test agreement between completeness scores and human judgments, residual equivalent-mutant noise, reasoning-effort sensitivity and cost-effectiveness. Appendix G adds successful specification examples, while Appendix H expands the earlier brief failure analysis into detailed cases. Existing control-flow and transformation-robustness analyses are retained.

E5.justification: Section 3.2 introduces plus/minus reporting for completeness scores and Cohen's kappa for human agreement. The meaning of the plus/minus quantities is unspecified. Neither version reports seeds, repeated-run counts or confidence intervals for the main LLM benchmark.

E6.justification: V4 adds substantial results for the additional models and reasoning settings; o3-mini high reasoning reports 10.6% success and 97.2% completeness. New validation reports completeness scores of 0.91 ± 0.08 versus 0.77 ± 0.19, kappa 0.72, and 3 equivalent mutants among 232. Cost findings and specification examples are also added. Clearly matched existing Table 1 rows, Table 2 and the original plotted results retain their values.

T1.justification: Definitions 1-2 and Appendix B's success, failure, completeness, flip-rate and normalization formulas are retained. No substantive mathematical assumptions, derivations, theorems or proofs are added or revised.

C1.justification: The abstract explicitly frames specification inference as a proxy for semantic reasoning, and the conclusion changes the stated evaluation scope from eight to 14 LLMs. The core benchmark contribution, limited semantic reasoning and robustness findings, and approximately 25% self-repair improvement claim remain.

C2.justification: V4 substantially expands the interpretation of benchmark validity and model behavior: it attributes most unknown outcomes to insufficient specification detail, argues that human agreement supports the completeness proxy, and discusses reasoning-training benefits and cost tradeoffs. Section 7 adds an explicit Java/JML generalization limitation and qualifies equivalent-mutant concerns using the new audit.

D1.justification: V4 identifies the deployed distilled R1 checkpoints and explains their resource constraints. The cost-analysis footnote discloses retrospective tracking and estimation from API pricing and token usage. Appendix C revises the DeepSeek identity, while tool versions, hardware descriptions, prompt templates and repository access information are otherwise retained.

R1.justification: V4 adds Jia and Harman's mutation-testing survey and Guo et al.'s DeepSeek-Coder reference, and removes the DeepSeek-V2 report. Section 5's research positioning remains essentially unchanged. The Le-Cong reference's preprint-to-publication update represents the same work.

P1.justification: V4 edits the abstract and prose, expands explanations of the metrics and failures, and inserts a successful-specifications appendix, shifting subsequent appendix labels. The main section order and most existing text remain intact. New unresolved 'Appendix ??' and 'XXX' placeholders reduce polish.

P2.justification: The visual presentation expands substantially through the enlarged Table 1, a new cost scatterplot in Figure 3 and numerous highlighted code listings in Appendices G-H, replacing the earlier single error-message listing. Existing plots retain their image content, with renumbering and reflow; the prompt boxes are relocated.

improvement.justification: The human-agreement check and equivalent-mutant audit provide useful empirical support for v1's completeness proxy. Additional model comparisons, cost analysis and worked examples also improve usefulness. These gains are limited by small, incompletely documented validation samples, inconsistent DeepSeek naming and unfinished appendix references/placeholders. The added evidence supports a modest net improvement without resolving the central measurement limitations.
